sources.title: Guide to the ADA Standards, Chapter 3: Floor and ground surfaces
sources.jurisdiction: United States (ADA Titles II and III)
sources.scope: Explains §§302–303: accessible floor surfaces must be stable, firm and slip resistant; the standards do not specify a minimum level of slip resistance; thick, cushioned or loose carpet impairs accessibility.
sources.limits: Guidance, not the enforceable text (see S28 and S30). U.S. only. Does not decide whether a site or element is covered.

sources.title: Slips and trips in retail
sources.scope: Slips and trips are the single most common cause of major injury in retail; contamination is implicated in almost all slip accidents; signs and cones only warn and do not stop people entering — use barriers, close doors or clean in sections; damp mopped smooth floors are very slippery.
sources.limits: British law and workplace context; used here only as operational practice, not as U.S. or Canadian law. No effect sizes.

sources.title: 29 CFR 1910.22 Walking-working surfaces: general requirements
sources.publisher: U.S. Occupational Safety and Health Administration
sources.jurisdiction: United States (federal OSHA; state plans may differ)
sources.scope: Walking-working surfaces kept clean, orderly and, to the extent feasible, dry; free of hazards such as leaks and spills; inspected regularly and as necessary; hazards corrected or guarded before employees use the surface again. No numerical coefficient of friction.
sources.limits: Protects employees, not customers. State-plan rules may be stricter.

sources.title: FDA Food Code (landing page)
sources.jurisdiction: United States (model code adopted by states, localities, tribes and territories)
sources.edition: 2026 edition is the most recent full edition (page current as of 2026-09-17)
sources.access: Landing page read; Chapter 6 text not audited
sources.scope: Regulators use the Food Code as a model for their own food-safety rules.
sources.limits: Not law until adopted; adopted editions and amendments vary. Floor-surface provisions must be confirmed in the locally adopted text.

sources.title: Codes Canada frequently asked questions (archived)
sources.scope: Historical explanation of how national model codes are adopted.
sources.limits: Historical; not a current register of provincial or territorial adoption.

sources.title: Codes Canada publications
sources.scope: Lists the 2025 National Building, Fire, Plumbing and Energy codes first; directs readers to provincial or territorial officials to find which codes apply.
sources.limits: Publication is not adoption; provinces and territories adopt, amend or replace model codes.

sources.title: ASTM F1292-26 Impact attenuation of surfacing materials within the use zone of playground equipment (public scope)
sources.access: Public scope only; licensed text not audited
sources.scope: Playground surfacing in the use zone of playground equipment; laboratory critical height or drop-height performance using g-max and HIC; laboratory results do not account for aging, moisture, maintenance or compaction; specific to the risk of head injury, with limited evidence for other serious injuries such as long-bone fractures.
sources.limits: Not a retail floor or fixture method; cannot certify retail safety.

sources.title: Mackey DC et al. (2019) FLIP randomized trial of compliant flooring in long-term care. PLoS Medicine 16(6): e1002843
sources.scope: 150 rooms randomized; 2.54 cm compliant underlay beneath vinyl versus plywood. Serious fall-related injury rate ratio 1.04 (95% CI 0.45–2.39); falls rate ratio 1.21 (0.87–1.68), i.e. a non-significant point estimate of more falls; adverse outcomes were not assessed.
sources.limits: Older adults in long-term care; one product and assembly. Low transferability to children in retail.

sources.title: Slip, trip and fall prevention (risk control services)
sources.scope: Risk-control consultants analyze past loss history, evaluate walking surfaces, premises use and maintenance, and can measure wet and dry slip resistance.
sources.limits: One company's service description; no premium discount or endorsement is stated or implied.

sources.title: ASTM F2508-23 Validation of walkway tribometry using research-based reference materials (public scope)
sources.access: Public scope only; licensed text not audited
sources.scope: Procedure for validating walkway tribometers against reference materials ranked by human subjects; explicitly not intended to establish a "safe" threshold for any walkway surface.
sources.limits: Validation practice only; does not convert readings into injury risk.

sources.title: ASTM E648-25a Critical radiant flux of floor-covering systems using a radiant heat energy source (public scope)
sources.jurisdiction: Voluntary consensus standard (adopted by reference in some codes)
sources.access: Public scope only; licensed text not audited
sources.scope: Measures critical radiant flux of horizontally mounted floor-covering systems; developed for corridors and exitways; not intended for routine estimation of flame spread elsewhere; does not by itself incorporate the factors needed for fire-hazard assessment.
sources.limits: Corrected in v3: version 2 cited an ASTM work-item page (WK95872) that does not name this standard. The required edition and class come from the adopted code and location.

sources.title: Flammable Fabrics Act business guidance (carpets and rugs, 16 CFR 1630/1631)
sources.scope: Parts 1630 and 1631 provide surface-flammability tests for large and small carpets and rugs exposed to a small ignition source; certificates of compliance are required.
sources.limits: Applies to carpets and rugs as defined; does not classify every resilient mat, foam tile or fixture padding.

sources.title: PIPEDA fair information principle 4: Limiting collection
sources.publisher: Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada
sources.scope: Collect only the personal information needed for a legitimate identified purpose, by fair and lawful means.
sources.limits: Not a determination of which privacy law applies (provincial laws may apply instead).

sources.title: ADA Update: A Primer for Small Business
sources.scope: Readily achievable barrier removal in existing facilities is a continuing duty; alterations must be accessible to the maximum extent feasible; temporary access interruptions must be remedied as soon as possible, and businesses should retrieve merchandise for customers who cannot get through a blocked aisle.
sources.limits: Guidance; does not decide a specific project.

sources.title: Prevention of slips, trips and falls
sources.publisher: Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety
sources.scope: Good housekeeping is the first and most important level of prevention; clean spills immediately; secure mats, rugs and carpets that do not lie flat.
sources.limits: Good practice; does not state provincial or territorial legal requirements.

sources.title: California Code of Regulations, Title 8, section 3273 ("Working Area")
sources.scope: Permanent floors and platforms free of dangerous projections or obstructions, maintained in good repair and reasonably free of oil, grease or water; slippery work surfaces protected with mats, grates, cleats or equivalent.
sources.limits: Worker protection; not a statement of duties to customers.

sources.title: Information Bulletin 25-01: 2025 California Building Standards Code effective date
sources.scope: 1 January 2026 is the statewide effective date; permit applications submitted on or after that date comply with the 2025 code; the 2022 code remains for applications received by 31 December 2025; local amendments must be ratified and filed for each edition.
sources.limits: Does not determine a specific project, local amendments or existing-building provisions.

sources.title: Accessibility in Ontario's Building Code
sources.access: Full page read (direct retrieval; v2 had only a search extract)
sources.scope: The 2024 Building Code defines accessibility requirements for most new construction and extensive renovations; existing buildings are not affected unless an extensive renovation is planned; the code works together with the Design of Public Spaces standard.
sources.limits: Guidance page; verify the regulation text, amendments and transition provisions.

sources.title: National Electronic Injury Surveillance System (NEISS)
sources.scope: Nationally representative probability sample of hospital emergency departments reporting consumer-product-related visits; national estimates from the sample.
sources.limits: Product-associated ED visits only; no store-visit denominators; product codes do not cover every scenario.

sources.title: Canadian Hospitals Injury Reporting and Prevention Program (CHIRPP)
sources.scope: Emergency-department injury surveillance at 20 sites (11 paediatric, 9 general); records what the person was doing, what went wrong and where the injury occurred.
sources.limits: Not representative of all injuries in Canada; urban paediatric hospitals over-represented; fatal injuries under-represented.

sources.title: Quality improvement activities FAQs
sources.publisher: U.S. HHS Office for Human Research Protections
sources.edition: Undated; issued before the 2018 Requirements took effect
sources.scope: Most quality-improvement efforts are not research subject to the HHS regulations; some are; intent to publish is an insufficient criterion for deciding.
sources.limits: Pre-2018 guidance; does not say who makes the determination; institutional policies apply.

sources.title: TCPS 2 (2022), Chapter 2: Scope and approach
sources.publisher: Panel on Research Ethics (Government of Canada)
sources.edition: TCPS 2 (2022), issued 2023-01-11; current edition per the policy page
sources.scope: Article 2.1 defines research; Article 2.5: quality assurance/improvement, program evaluation and performance reviews are not research under the policy; pilot studies fall within the definition of research requiring REB review.
sources.limits: Applies where the policy binds the institution; institutional REB decides.

sources.title: Tax benefits for businesses who have employees with disabilities
sources.scope: Disabled Access Credit (Form 8826) for small businesses that earned $1 million or less or had no more than 30 full-time employees in the previous year; barrier-removal deduction of up to $15,000 a year for qualified expenses removing architectural and transportation barriers.
sources.limits: No determination that this program or any flooring or padding expense qualifies.

sources.title: Guide to the ADA Standards, Chapter 3: Protruding objects
sources.scope: Objects with leading edges above the 27 in cane-detection height and below 80 in headroom are limited in how far they project into circulation paths (4 in); post-mounted objects 12 in; 80 in headroom.
sources.limits: Guidance; enforceable text in S28/S30.

sources.title: ASTM F2753-21 Effect of dynamic rolling load over resilient floor covering systems (public scope)
sources.access: Public scope only; licensed text not audited
sources.scope: Practice for determining the effect of dynamic rolling load on resilient floor coverings, including joints; intended for resilient, adhesive and underlayment manufacturers; diagnostic and comparative use.
sources.limits: No universal wheel or load acceptance value.

sources.title: CAN/ULC-S102.2-18 (R2024) Surface burning characteristics of flooring, floor coverings and miscellaneous materials (listing)
sources.edition: Edition 8 (2018), reaffirmed 2024; listing shows both "Archived" and "Active" labels
sources.scope: Compares flame spread and smoke developed values of floor surfaces and coverings and of materials that cannot be tested under CAN/ULC-S102.
sources.limits: Does not set performance requirements for specific uses; listing status should be confirmed; code professional decides edition, class and location.

sources.title: CSA/ASC B651:23 Accessible design for the built environment (summary)
sources.scope: Requirements for making buildings and facilities accessible to people with physical, sensory and cognitive disabilities; referenced in the National Building Code and other legislation.
sources.limits: Whether it binds a site depends on the adopting instrument; technical text not audited.

sources.title: 36 CFR part 1191, appendix D — ADA technical requirements §§302, 303, 307, 403 (unofficial copy)
sources.publisher: Legal Information Institute (copy of U.S. Access Board regulation)
sources.scope: 302.1 floor surfaces stable, firm and slip resistant; 302.2 carpet securely attached with firm cushion, pad or backing or none, pile ≤ 1/2 in (13 mm), exposed edges fastened with trim; 302.3 openings pass no sphere > 1/2 in; 303 changes in level ≤ 1/4 in vertical, 1/4–1/2 in bevelled no steeper than 1:2, > 1/2 in ramped; 307.2 objects with leading edges 27–80 in (685–2030 mm) protrude ≤ 4 in (100 mm); 307.4 headroom 80 in; 307.5 protruding objects shall not reduce required clear width; 403.5.1 clear width 36 in (915 mm), reducible to 32 in (815 mm) for ≤ 24 in (610 mm).
sources.limits: Unofficial copy — confirm against the official DOJ 2010 Standards (S30) or eCFR before citing in a compliance file. Scoping (which elements must comply) is set elsewhere.

sources.title: 28 CFR 36.211 Maintenance of accessible features
sources.jurisdiction: United States (ADA Title III public accommodations)
sources.edition: eCFR up to date as of 2026-10-16
sources.scope: Public accommodations maintain accessible features in operable working condition; isolated or temporary interruptions in service or access due to maintenance or repairs are not prohibited.
sources.limits: Does not define how long "temporary" may be; see DOJ guidance (S14).

sources.title: 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design
sources.jurisdiction: United States (ADA Titles II and III)
sources.edition: Published 2010-09-15 with the revised Title II and III regulations
sources.access: Introductory sections read (chapter text via S28)
sources.scope: Identifies the 2010 Standards as the DOJ regulations plus the 2004 ADAAG (36 CFR part 1191, appendices B and D).
sources.limits: Retrieval of chapters 3–4 was truncated in this environment; technical text was read through S28.

sources.title: Martin K, Chounthirath T, Xiang H, Smith GA (2014) Pediatric shopping-cart-related injuries treated in US emergency departments, 1990–2011. Clinical Pediatrics 53(3):277–285
sources.publisher: Clinical Pediatrics (peer reviewed); abstract via PCOM Digital Commons
sources.scope: An estimated 530,494 children under 15 were treated in U.S. emergency departments for shopping-cart injuries over 1990–2011 (about 24,113 a year); the head was injured in 78.1%; the concussion/closed-head-injury rate rose 213% (0.64 to 2.02 per 10,000); numbers did not decline after the 2004 cart standard.
sources.limits: Abstract-level reading; surveillance estimates without store-visit denominators; diagnostic trends can affect concussion counts.

sources.title: O'Brien CW (2009) Shopping cart injuries to children under five, 2003–2008
sources.publisher: U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission, Directorate for Epidemiology
sources.scope: About 121,989 emergency-department-treated injuries 2003–2008 (95% CI 101,115–142,863); 2006–2008 annual average 21,065; falls from carts 82%, tip-overs 4%; head/face 84%; hospitalized 3%; ages one and two 59%; reported incidents included broken or missing restraint straps and car seats falling from carts.
sources.limits: Older data (2003–2008); estimates carry sampling error; no store denominators.

sources.title: ASTM F2372-15(2021) Consumer safety performance specification for shopping carts (public scope)
sources.access: Public scope only; licensed text not audited
sources.scope: Performance requirements, test methods and labelling for shopping carts and restraint systems for children at least six months and 15 lb up to four years and 35 lb; excludes infant carriers.
sources.limits: Voluntary; applies to cart design, not to how carts are used or maintained in a store.

sources.title: Study finds safety intervention increases use of child safety restraints in shopping carts (news release on a 2006 Pediatrics study)
sources.access: News release read; primary article not retrieved
sources.scope: Three intervention and four comparison stores; greeters encouraged restraint use and caregivers received a coupon; correct restraint use in intervention stores rose from 15% to 49%; about half of children remained unrestrained or incorrectly restrained; injuries were not measured.
sources.limits: Secondary source; process outcome only; sample sizes and comparison figures not reported in the release.

sources.title: Lachance CC et al. (2017) Compliant flooring to prevent fall-related injuries in older adults: a scoping review. PLoS ONE 12(2): e0171652
sources.scope: Compliant flooring reduced fall-related impact forces in laboratory studies; may reduce injuries but may increase fall risk; clinical evidence was small studies without a powered trial; most workplace-safety records found more force was needed to push, pull or turn carts, beds, wheelchairs and lifts.
sources.limits: Older-adult and health-care evidence; no risk-of-bias assessment; predates the FLIP results (S8).

sources.title: Bell J et al. (2008) Evaluation of a comprehensive slip, trip, and fall prevention program for hospital employees (NOIRS 2008 abstract)
sources.publisher: National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (CDC Stacks)
sources.scope: A multi-component program (injury-record analysis, hazard assessments, housekeeping changes, flooring changes, ice and snow removal, footwear for some groups) was followed by a 58% fall in workers' compensation slip, trip and fall claims, adjusted rate ratio 0.42 (95% CI 0.33–0.54); liquid contamination was the most common cause.
sources.limits: Employees, not customers; before/after design without a comparison group described; footwear components do not transfer to customers.

sources.title: WHO Child Growth Standards: height-for-age percentiles, boys and girls 2–5 years
sources.edition: WHO Child Growth Standards (percentile tables, PDF)
sources.access: Boys and girls 2–5 year percentile tables read
sources.scope: 97th-percentile height: boys 92.9 cm at 2 years and 118.7 cm at 5 years; girls 91.8 cm and 118.4 cm. 3rd percentile at 2 years: boys 81.4 cm, girls 79.6 cm.
sources.limits: Height, not head or eye height; used only to set a program survey band. Older children need a 5–19 year reference.

sources.title: ASTM F1637-21 Standard practice for safe walking surfaces (public scope)
sources.access: Public scope only; licensed text not audited
sources.scope: Design and construction guidelines and minimum maintenance criteria for walking surfaces in new and existing buildings, for pedestrians in ordinary footwear; may not be adequate for people with certain mobility impairments; conformance will not remove all hazards.
sources.limits: Voluntary practice; applicability is a program or contract decision unless adopted by law.

sources.title: ANSI A326.3-2021 Dynamic coefficient of friction (DCOF) of hard surface flooring materials (listing)
sources.publisher: ANSI Webstore (content provider: Tile Council of North America)
sources.edition: A326.3-2021 (revises 2017 edition); most recent per listing
sources.access: Listing read; full text not audited
sources.scope: Describes a DCOF test method for hard surface flooring and includes DCOF specifications, product-use classifications and guidance on specifying.
sources.limits: Hard-surface flooring only; specification values were not audited here and are not a guarantee of in-use safety.

sources.title: ANSI/ASSP A1264.2-2022 Reducing slip missteps on walking-working surfaces (listing)
sources.publisher: ANSI Webstore (content provider: American Society of Safety Professionals)
sources.access: Listing read; full text not audited
sources.scope: Provisions for reducing the risk of slip missteps in workplace situations, for safety, design and facility professionals.
sources.limits: Workplace scope; numeric values, if any, not audited.

sources.title: 45 CFR 46.102 Definitions for purposes of the human subjects policy
sources.jurisdiction: United States (federally conducted or supported research and institutions that apply it)
sources.edition: eCFR up to date as of 2026-10-15
sources.scope: Research is a systematic investigation, including research development, testing and evaluation, designed to develop or contribute to generalizable knowledge; a human subject involves interaction/intervention or identifiable private information.
sources.limits: Applicability of part 46 depends on funding and institutional assurances (46.101, not retrieved).

sources.title: Guidelines for overt video surveillance in the private sector
sources.publisher: Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada
sources.scope: Consider less privacy-invasive alternatives first; use surveillance only for its stated purpose; notify the public before entry; secure recordings and limit access; delete when no longer needed; review periodically.
sources.limits: Guidance, not law; the binding sources are PIPEDA and provincial private-sector laws.

sources.title: How to make customer service accessible (temporary disruptions)
sources.edition: Page updated 2026-09-21; refers to O. Reg. 191/11
sources.scope: When accessible facilities or services are temporarily out of service, give public notice stating the reason, how long, and any alternative; post at the entrance or another high-traffic area, or on the website or phone line.
sources.limits: Guidance page; the regulation text (e-Laws) could not be retrieved in this environment.

sources.title: The FDA releases 2026 Food Code
sources.publisher: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (constituent update)
sources.scope: Announces the 2026 edition on 17 September 2026; adoption by state, local, tribal and territorial agencies is voluntary.
sources.limits: Announcement; does not cover floor-surface provisions.

sources.title: Falls (fact sheet)
sources.scope: Falls are the second leading cause of unintentional injury death worldwide (an estimated 684 000 deaths a year); nearly 40% of the disability-adjusted life years lost to falls worldwide occur in children; children are named as a high-risk group, with falls linked to developmental stages, supervision and hazardous environments; prevention should emphasise education, training, safer environments, research and policy.
sources.limits: Global estimates across all settings, mostly homes and daily life; no retail-specific data. Published 2021: check for a newer edition before quoting.

sources.title: World report on child injury prevention, chapter 1: Child injuries in context
sources.publisher: World Health Organization and UNICEF (NCBI Bookshelf copy); editors Peden M, Oyegbite K, Ozanne-Smith J and others
sources.access: Chapter 1 read (first 100 000 characters); the dedicated falls chapter could not be opened because the site showed a browser check
sources.scope: Falls are leading causes of non-fatal child injury but a small share of fatal child injuries; standards, product design and environmental modification are named prevention approaches; the chapter notes there was insufficient trial evidence that environmental changes in homes reduce the number of injuries.
sources.limits: Published 2008; general and home settings, not retail. The falls chapter was not reviewed here.

sources.title: Preventable injuries kill 2000 children every day (news release on the World report on child injury prevention)
sources.scope: Falls are one of the five leading causes of child injury death in the 2008 estimate (nearly 47 000 child deaths a year), with hundreds of thousands more less serious fall injuries; proven measures listed include standards and redesigning nursery furniture, toys and playground equipment.
sources.limits: 2008 estimates; a news summary of the report, not the report itself.

sources.title: Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities (articles 4 and 9)
sources.publisher: United Nations, Office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights
sources.scope: Article 9 requires States Parties to take measures for access to the physical environment and to facilities and services open to the public, including minimum accessibility standards and ensuring that private entities offering facilities open to the public take accessibility into account; article 4(3) requires close consultation with persons with disabilities, including children with disabilities, through their representative organizations.
sources.limits: Obligations fall on States Parties, not directly on businesses; ratification and national implementation vary. Check the country's status and its own laws.

sources.title: Sustainable Development Goal 11: targets 11.2 and 11.7
sources.publisher: United Nations Department of Economic and Social Affairs
sources.type: UN goal, target and indicator text
sources.scope: Target 11.7: by 2030, provide universal access to safe, inclusive and accessible, green and public spaces, in particular for women and children, older persons and persons with disabilities.
sources.limits: Indicator 11.7.1 measures urban open space for public use, which privately run shops are not. Use as policy context, never as a business obligation.

sources.title: ISO 21542:2021 Building construction — Accessibility and usability of the built environment
sources.jurisdiction: International voluntary standard (applies where adopted or referenced)
sources.access: Public scope page only; standard text not purchased
sources.scope: Requirements and recommendations for construction elements, fittings and products that affect getting into, moving within and leaving buildings, including evacuation; also applies to common spaces in multi-unit residential buildings.
sources.limits: Text not audited; national adoption varies; does not address child impact injuries specifically.

sources.title: ISO/IEC Guide 50:2014 Safety aspects — Guidelines for child safety in standards and other specifications
sources.publisher: International Electrotechnical Commission webstore (joint ISO/IEC guide)
sources.scope: Guidance for experts who develop and revise standards and specifications on potential sources of bodily harm to children from products they use or are likely to come into contact with, even if the products are not intended for children; intentional and non-physical harm are out of scope.
sources.limits: Abstract only; written for standards developers, not for sites; sets no thresholds.

sources.title: ISO/IEC Guide 71:2014 Guide for addressing accessibility in standards
sources.scope: Guidance to standards developers on addressing accessibility requirements and recommendations in standards for products, services and built environments.
sources.limits: Not a site requirement; text not audited.

sources.title: ISO 7010:2019 Graphical symbols — Safety colours and safety signs — Registered safety signs
sources.jurisdiction: International voluntary standard (applies where adopted or referenced)
sources.edition: Edition 3, 2019-07, with amendments 1 to 11 (2020–2026); a revision is in progress
sources.scope: Prescribes registered safety signs for accident prevention, fire protection, health hazard information and emergency evacuation, for all locations where safety issues related to people need to be addressed.
sources.limits: Sign catalogue not reviewed; national sign rules and languages may differ. A sign warns; it does not control a hazard.

sources.title: Statement for World Day for Safety and Health at Work 2025 (ILO Office for Türkiye)
sources.scope: States that in 2022 the International Labour Conference amended the ILO Declaration to add a safe and healthy working environment as a fifth fundamental principle, and that Conventions No. 155 and No. 187 are now considered fundamental conventions.
sources.limits: A statement about the 2022 decision, not the Declaration itself; national ratification and law vary.

sources.title: Injury surveillance guidelines
sources.publisher: World Health Organization (with experts from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)
sources.access: Publication page read; manual not reviewed in full
sources.scope: Practical advice for researchers and practitioners on developing information systems that collect systematic injury data, including where resources, staff or equipment are limited.
sources.limits: 2001 guidance; does not cover retail exposure measures or current privacy law.

sources.title: Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.2
sources.jurisdiction: International technical standard (referenced by many laws and policies)
sources.access: Status and selected success criteria read
sources.scope: Success criteria for accessible web content, including 2.2.2 Pause, Stop, Hide and 2.3.3 Animation from Interactions, which shaped this workspace's motion controls.
sources.limits: This package has not been audited for conformance; automated scans cover only some criteria.

evidence.claim: Contamination is implicated in almost all retail slip accidents; cleaning itself can create slippery floors
evidence.transfer: Mechanism plausible for children; no effect size
evidence.implication: Prioritize source control, cleaning method and response time

evidence.claim: Signs and cones only warn of a hazard; they do not prevent entry
evidence.transfer: Directly relevant: children do not read signs
evidence.implication: Isolation means a physical barrier or closure plus an accessible alternative

evidence.claim: ADA accessible surfaces must be stable, firm and slip resistant; no minimum friction value is set
evidence.setting: U.S. sites covered by the ADA
evidence.transfer: Applies to all visitors including children with disabilities
evidence.basis: Regulation text (unofficial copy) and agency guide
evidence.limits: Coverage and stricter local rules decided locally
evidence.implication: Do not cite an "ADA friction number"; specialists set method-specific thresholds

evidence.claim: ADA carpet rules: securely attached, firm or no cushion, pile ≤ 1/2 in, exposed edges trimmed
evidence.limits: Whether a product is "carpet" and whether the area is covered must be decided
evidence.implication: Soft or cushioned coverings on routes need access review before purchase

evidence.claim: ADA changes in level: ≤ 1/4 in vertical; ≤ 1/2 in bevelled at 1:2 maximum; larger changes ramped
evidence.transfer: Applies to mat, underlay and padding edges
evidence.implication: Measure every new edge and transition at commissioning

evidence.claim: ADA protruding objects: 27–80 in leading edges protrude ≤ 4 in; protrusions may not reduce required clear width; 80 in headroom
evidence.implication: Check guard thickness at the real fixture

evidence.claim: ADA accessible route clear width 36 in, reducible to 32 in for ≤ 24 in
evidence.transfer: Padding on aisle fixtures can narrow routes
evidence.limits: Other width rules (turns, passing spaces) also apply
evidence.implication: Measure route width after guards are fitted

evidence.claim: Accessible features must be maintained; isolated or temporary interruptions for maintenance or repair are allowed; DOJ expects merchandise retrieval when an aisle is blocked
evidence.transfer: Shapes how closures and isolations are run
evidence.implication: Isolation procedure includes assistance and prompt reopening

evidence.claim: U.S. employers must inspect walking-working surfaces and correct or guard hazards before employees use them; no friction number
evidence.implication: Use as the worker-safety floor; customer duties need counsel

evidence.claim: Ontario guidance: give public notice of temporary disruptions to accessible facilities, with reason, duration and alternatives
evidence.transfer: Applies to closures during installation or isolation
evidence.implication: Add notices to the installation and closure procedures for Ontario sites

evidence.claim: Tribometer validation (F2508-23) is not intended to establish a safe threshold
evidence.implication: Thresholds must be set by specialists before testing

evidence.claim: Playground surfacing test F1292-26 is specific to head-injury risk in playground use zones; laboratory results ignore aging and maintenance
evidence.implication: Never cite playground certification for retail floors or fixtures

evidence.claim: Floor-covering fire method E648-25a was developed for corridors and exitways and is not alone a fire-hazard assessment
evidence.limits: Required class comes from the adopted code
evidence.implication: Fixture padding needs its own code determination

evidence.claim: A randomized trial of compliant flooring found no effect on serious fall injuries; falls were non-significantly higher; harms were not assessed
evidence.setting: Older adults, one long-term care site
evidence.implication: Do not claim cushioning efficacy for children or retail

evidence.claim: Compliant flooring reduces laboratory impact forces but may raise fall risk and increases force to move wheeled equipment
evidence.implication: Rolling effort and stability are pass/fail criteria

evidence.claim: An average of about 24,000 U.S. children under 15 a year were treated in emergency departments for shopping-cart injuries (1990–2011); most involved the head
evidence.implication: Route cart controls to an owner (task T35) before buying floor products

evidence.claim: For children under five, falls from carts were 82% of cart injuries and tip-overs 4%; 84% involved the head or face
evidence.implication: Prioritize restraint use and cart condition

evidence.claim: Cart-related concussion/closed-head-injury rates rose 1990–2011 and totals did not fall after the 2004 cart standard
evidence.implication: A design standard alone is not enough; operational controls matter

evidence.claim: The shopping-cart standard F2372-15(2021) covers carts and restraints for children 6 months–4 years and excludes infant carriers
evidence.implication: Use as a procurement criterion when replacing carts

evidence.claim: A store-entrance intervention raised correct cart-restraint use from 15% to 49%; about half remained unrestrained
evidence.limits: Injuries not measured; primary article not retrieved
evidence.implication: Candidate operational control to evaluate, not an injury claim

evidence.claim: A multi-component hospital-employee program was followed by 58% fewer slip, trip and fall claims
evidence.transfer: Partial: housekeeping parts may transfer; footwear does not
evidence.implication: Supports operational controls; not a customer estimate

evidence.claim: No controlled study of retail edge guards or corner padding was found in this targeted review
evidence.implication: Treat guards as an untested residual-hazard option

evidence.claim: WHO 97th-percentile height is about 92–93 cm at age two and 118–119 cm at age five
evidence.implication: Basis for the survey band below

evidence.claim: Survey fixture edges from the floor to at least 120 cm for ages two to five
evidence.limits: Raise for older children; not a legal requirement
evidence.implication: Use in the hazard walk (document 28)

evidence.claim: Use a 90-day operational feasibility window after commissioning
evidence.implication: Agree locally; extend if needed

evidence.claim: At 2 events per 100,000 entries, detecting a 20% reduction needs about 355 comparison events (about 17.7 million entries per arm)
evidence.basis: Normal approximation for a log rate ratio
evidence.implication: A single-site pilot cannot support an injury-reduction claim

evidence.claim: 15,000 initial cost and 20,000 retained loss scenario
evidence.implication: Replace with quotes and validated loss data

evidence.claim: Local injury reduction and insurance savings
evidence.implication: No public benefit claim; premium changes excluded from models

evidence.claim: U.S. disabled-access tax mechanisms exist with eligibility limits (credit for small businesses; deduction up to $15,000 a year)
evidence.limits: Eligibility of this work not established
evidence.implication: Tax review before any budget recognition

evidence.claim: Research is defined by systematic investigation for generalizable knowledge (U.S.); TCPS 2 treats pilot studies as research requiring REB review
evidence.implication: Obtain a determination before structured testing or evaluation

evidence.claim: Video surveillance: consider less intrusive alternatives, limit to purpose, notify, secure and delete
evidence.implication: No new CCTV for this program; footage stays in protected systems

evidence.claim: Code editions depend on adoption and timing (2025 California code for permits from 1 Jan 2026; Ontario 2024 code for new construction and extensive renovation; 2025 national model codes published)
evidence.limits: Local amendments and project scope decide
evidence.implication: Record edition and basis per requirement in the jurisdiction register

evidence.claim: The FDA Food Code 2026 edition was released on 17 September 2026 as a model code
evidence.limits: Adoption varies; floor provisions not audited
evidence.implication: Health authority confirms the adopted text for food zones

evidence.claim: Falls are the second leading cause of unintentional injury death worldwide, and nearly 40% of the disability-adjusted life years lost to falls occur in children
evidence.transfer: Shows the scale of child falls; says nothing about retail's share
evidence.implication: Child falls are a legitimate public-health priority; measure the retail share locally before claiming it

evidence.claim: Falls are a leading cause of non-fatal child injury but account for a small share of child injury deaths
evidence.transfer: Supports measuring non-fatal outcomes; retail share unknown
evidence.basis: WHO/UNICEF report chapter and news release
evidence.implication: Plan evaluations around non-fatal injuries and hazards, not deaths

evidence.claim: In 2008 there was insufficient trial evidence that environmental changes in homes reduce the number of child injuries
evidence.transfer: Caution transfers: environmental change is plausible but unproven
evidence.implication: Present site changes as reasonable precautions under evaluation, never as proven injury reductions

evidence.claim: CRPD States Parties must take measures so that facilities open to the public, including privately run ones, take accessibility into account, and must consult disabled people, including disabled children
evidence.limits: Obligations fall on States, not businesses; ratification and national law vary
evidence.implication: No child-safety change may reduce access; consult disability organizations before changing a site

evidence.claim: A safe and healthy working environment has been an ILO fundamental principle since 2022
evidence.transfer: Retail cleaning, cart handling and ergonomics
evidence.implication: Worker safety is part of every assessment, not a side issue

evidence.claim: ISO 21542 (building accessibility) and ISO/IEC Guide 50 (child safety in product standards) are useful reference points; their public scopes do not describe retail child-impact thresholds
evidence.implication: Cite them as references in local reviews; never as an approval or a threshold

workflows.title: Open the bundle and set up the workspace
workflows.trigger: First use of the bundle, a new device or browser, or a new version.
workflows.prerequisites: The full ZIP extracted to an approved folder; one assigned editor.
workflows.inputs: The bundle; a non-identifying site code; an approved backup location.
steps: Open index.html (or standalone.html) and check the storage indicator in the status bar at the bottom of the page.
Enter the non-identifying site profile in the Implementation plan.
Export the first planning backup to the approved location and name it with the date.
Re-import that backup to see the validation preview, then cancel.
Record the browser and result in the software-acceptance register (source/MANUAL-CHECKS.md).
workflows.outputs: A dated backup file; a software-acceptance row.
workflows.acceptance: The indicator shows "Saved in this browser" (or you have chosen to work from exports); the backup preview opens without errors.
workflows.escalation: Storage unavailable or blocked: keep working and export before closing. Pages do not load: try standalone.html, then ask IT. Never bypass device or browser security settings.

workflows.title: Appoint owners, scope and charter (G0)
workflows.trigger: A decision to explore the program at one or more sites.
workflows.prerequisites: A sponsor willing to hold stop and withdrawal authority.
workflows.inputs: Site list, organization chart, budget envelope, existing safety procedures.
steps: Name the sponsor, site lead, facilities owner, evaluation lead and deputies (T01).
Define sites, jurisdiction and scope, including exclusions and adjacent mechanisms (T02).
Propose assessment budget and removal-reserve approach for signature (T03).
Adopt the charter, responsibility matrix and decision rights (document 10; document 49) (T05).
Record the G0 decision reference after the signed record exists.
workflows.outputs: Signed charter in the controlled system; G0 decision row.
workflows.acceptance: T01–T05 have dispositions with evidence references; the G0 note cites the signed record.
workflows.escalation: No sponsor accepts stop authority: do not proceed beyond ordinary hazard correction. Budget refused: continue W03/W04 only.

workflows.title: Initial hazard walk, immediate controls and routing
workflows.trigger: Day 1; any layout, product, season or traffic change; a reported concern.
workflows.prerequisites: Existing safety and emergency procedures; barriers and supplies available.
workflows.inputs: Floor plan, the 0–120 cm child survey band (document 28), cart-fleet status, hazard checklist.
steps: Walk every zone at opening, peak, cleaning and restocking where safely feasible, with facilities and a worker representative.
Record each observable condition in the hazard register — never people's details.
Isolate critical conditions at once with a physical barrier and an accessible alternative; offer assistance.
Take defective carts out of service and log them.
Assign owners and due dates in the action register.
Route carts, tip-over, falling merchandise, doors and escalators to their accountable owners (T35).
workflows.outputs: Hazard and action rows; routing decisions for adjacent mechanisms.
workflows.acceptance: Every critical condition is isolated with an owner and verification; no hazard is kept for research; every adjacent mechanism has a named owner.
workflows.escalation: No capacity to repair: tell the sponsor the same day. Regulated systems (egress, fire protection, structure) affected: landlord and the authority.

workflows.title: Daily inspection, spill response and reopening
workflows.authority: Shift lead isolates; the designated role reopens after verification
workflows.trigger: Scheduled inspection, a spill or contamination report, cleaning, restocking or weather.
workflows.prerequisites: Trained responder and deputy on shift; approved cleaning methods; barriers.
workflows.inputs: Inspection schedule, approved chemicals and dilution, spill kit.
steps: Protect people: physically block entry and keep an accessible alternative.
Offer assistance (for example, retrieve goods from a closed aisle).
Identify the hazard; call a specialist for unknown chemicals or blood.
Clean and fix the source with the approved method; keep the area closed while wet.
Verify dryness, residue, seams and guards before reopening.
Log the four timestamps; hand over open items at shift change (W16).
workflows.outputs: Spill-response and inspection rows; handoff rows.
workflows.acceptance: All four timestamps recorded; reopening verified by the authorized role; recurring sources escalated.
workflows.escalation: Recurring source or overdue repair: site manager the same shift. Product defect: suspend under W11.

workflows.title: Baseline data, exposure and evidence plan (G1)
workflows.authority: Privacy officer (data access); research-ethics office (if research)
workflows.inputs: De-identified aggregate incident counts, visitor counts and their methods, the evidence ledger.
steps: Ask the privacy officer which aggregate data may be shared and how.
Request a research or quality-improvement determination before any structured study.
Enter aggregate counts and exposure by period; record missing exposure.
Use Evaluation planning to see what the data can and cannot show.
Record evidence gaps and lock a pre-analysis plan (T09, T10).
workflows.outputs: Aggregate-outcome rows; evidence rows; determination references.
workflows.acceptance: Event and exposure windows match; missingness documented; no identifiable data in the workspace; determinations recorded.
workflows.escalation: Identifiable data offered or requested: stop and refer to the privacy officer. Determination refused or pending: operational controls only.

workflows.title: Community, disability and worker consultation
workflows.authority: Ethics office if the activity is research; sponsor for compensation
workflows.trigger: Before selecting products, and before any physical pilot.
workflows.prerequisites: Accessible formats; compensation arrangements; privacy notice.
steps: Invite adult advisors through accessible, voluntary and compensated channels.
Explain recording, retention and withdrawal before participation.
Record themes and objections without personal details.
Feed barriers into the hazard and action registers.
workflows.acceptance: Each group's themes and objections recorded; responses assigned owners.
workflows.escalation: Structured testing proposed: obtain an ethics determination first. Advisor raises a safety concern: treat as a hazard report (W03).

workflows.title: Jurisdiction, permits, landlord and insurer routing (G2)
workflows.authority: Authorities having jurisdiction; landlord; insurer (each within its remit)
workflows.trigger: A proposed physical change, or before any procurement commitment.
workflows.prerequisites: An exact work scope and site profile.
steps: List every requirement as LAW, CONTRACT, PROGRAM or PROPOSAL with citation, edition and reviewer.
Send the authority consultation request (document 07) and record answers as advice or binding conditions.
Obtain landlord consent and responsibility allocation in writing.
Ask the insurer for policy-specific notice and conditions in writing.
workflows.outputs: Jurisdiction and consultation rows; written determinations.
workflows.acceptance: Every requirement has type, citation, edition and reviewer; every "not applicable" has a reason; written determinations exist for regulated work.
workflows.escalation: Conflicting advice: code professional or counsel decides. Silence: treat as unresolved, never as approval.

workflows.title: Option selection and acceptance criteria (G3, part 1)
workflows.authority: Competent specialists approve criteria before any test
workflows.trigger: G2 pathway known for the proposed work.
workflows.prerequisites: Hazard mechanisms documented; intervention library reviewed.
steps: Compare elimination, repair, redesign, operational and protective options for each mechanism.
Write acceptance criteria for the whole installed system with method, edition and threshold basis.
Have specialists approve thresholds before any test is ordered.
Record candidate methods and required editions in the standards register.
workflows.outputs: Selection worksheet; product-acceptance, test-plan and standards rows.
workflows.acceptance: Every mandatory criterion is pass/fail with an approved threshold or qualitative condition set before testing.
workflows.escalation: No competent specialist available: no protective installation; continue ordinary controls.

workflows.title: Procurement, dossier and mock-up (G3, part 2)
workflows.authority: Sponsor signs the award after mandatory criteria pass
workflows.inputs: Statement of work (document 39), RFI (document 09), acceptance schedule.
steps: Issue the RFI/SOW with the acceptance schedule.
Pass/fail mandatory criteria before scoring.
Run the mock-up with loaded carts, mobility devices and the actual cleaning routine.
Commission an independent review of reports; resolve critical gaps.
Finalize contract, budget and restoration plan for signature (T20).
workflows.outputs: Dossier; mock-up records; signed award in the controlled record.
workflows.acceptance: All mandatory criteria pass; no critical criterion undetermined; removal funded.
workflows.escalation: Supplier withholds data: exclude the bid. Mock-up fails: return to W08.

workflows.title: Installation, commissioning and go/no-go (G4)
workflows.authority: Site manager and facilities sign the release; authorities inspect where required; sponsor decides go/no-go
workflows.trigger: Signed award and approvals in place.
workflows.prerequisites: G0–G3 complete; permits; landlord consent; notice of temporary disruption where required.
workflows.inputs: Approved drawings and assembly; commissioning checklist (document 11).
steps: Enforce installer hold points; record batches and deviations.
Repeat the approved slip-resistance check in situ; measure route widths, protrusions and transitions.
Demonstrate mobility aids, strollers, loaded carts and cleaning with consenting adults.
Demonstrate staff competency on every shift (T23).
Confirm maintenance, data and withdrawal readiness (T24).
Hold the go/no-go review and record signed releases (T25).
workflows.outputs: Commissioning and asset rows; signed release and go/no-go decision.
workflows.acceptance: Every commissioning criterion passes; no critical defect open; training demonstrated; removal reserve available.
workflows.escalation: Any critical defect: no public use. A no-go condition in document 48: decision is "no-go" regardless of schedule.

workflows.title: Stop, isolate, suspend or withdraw
workflows.owner: Any trained worker starts; site manager suspends; sponsor withdraws
workflows.trigger: A stop trigger in document 14, or any concern that a system is unsafe.
workflows.prerequisites: None — protective action never waits for proof of causation.
workflows.inputs: Stop triggers; isolation equipment; contact sheet.
steps: Isolate the area and keep an accessible alternative.
Notify the shift lead and site manager; use the emergency process for any injury.
Site manager suspends the affected installation.
Record the decision with a coded incident reference.
Check other sites with the same batch or assembly.
Sponsor decides permanent withdrawal if the risk cannot be corrected.
workflows.outputs: Decision row; incident reference in the protected system; asset status.
workflows.acceptance: The area is isolated promptly; the decision is recorded; affected batches are checked.
workflows.escalation: Serious injury: emergency services, then legal/claims contacts under existing policy.

workflows.title: Correct and restart
workflows.authority: Site manager and facilities; accessibility reviewer for access issues; authority where required; sponsor for pilot continuation
workflows.trigger: A suspended system with a proposed correction.
steps: Record the root cause and the proposed correction in change control.
Retest against the pre-agreed criteria — never new criteria chosen after results.
Retrain staff and revise the procedure.
Collect the required signatures and record the restart decision.
workflows.outputs: Change-control and decision rows; retest report reference.
workflows.acceptance: Retest passes the pre-agreed criteria; signatures recorded; staff retrained.

workflows.title: Pilot operation and review (G5)
workflows.authority: Steering group; independent reviewer for assurance
workflows.prerequisites: Protocol, data flow and determinations in place.
workflows.inputs: Weekly logs, aggregate outcomes, audit checklist (document 40).
steps: Inspect after the first trading and cleaning cycles.
Review defects, complaints and data quality weekly.
Hold 30- and 60-day operational and budget reviews.
Analyze results and balancing outcomes with the evaluation lead.
Commission an independent assurance review.
workflows.outputs: Weekly and monthly reports; audit findings; independent review.
workflows.acceptance: Locally adopted feasibility criteria assessed honestly; adverse findings reported.
workflows.escalation: Critical finding: W11. Data invalid: report as invalid, do not compute rates.

workflows.title: Scale, extend, redesign or remove (G6)
workflows.inputs: Document 25 evidence table; cost scenarios; decision record.
steps: Assemble the evidence summary, including adverse results and costs.
Answer the G6 questions in document 25.
Choose stop, revise, extend or staged scale, with the evidence each option needs.
Fund maintenance, replacement and withdrawal before any expansion.
Record conditions, dissent and the next review date.
workflows.outputs: Signed decision memo; budget; replication plan.
workflows.acceptance: The decision matches the evidence: feasibility alone never supports an injury-reduction claim.
workflows.escalation: Evidence insufficient: extend evaluation rather than scale.

workflows.title: Public claims and outreach
workflows.authority: Communications and evaluation leads; legal for material claims
workflows.trigger: Any planned public statement, notice or outreach message.
steps: Draft the statement from dated records only.
Check for prohibited claims ("childproof", "zero risk", "certified safe", unsupported percentages, implied endorsements).
Record evidence, scope limit and decision in the publication-claims register.
Publish only approved statements through authorized channels.
workflows.acceptance: Every statement is tied to a dated record and approved; no prohibited claim.
workflows.escalation: Evidence missing: reject or revise the statement.

workflows.title: Handoffs between shifts, contractors, tenants and roles
workflows.trigger: Shift change, contractor visit end, tenant or provider change, role change.
steps: List open hazards, isolated zones, temporary routes and next required actions.
Hand over in person or by the approved channel.
Incoming lead acknowledges and records the time.
workflows.acceptance: Every open hazard has an acknowledged owner.
workflows.escalation: Not acknowledged: the outgoing lead keeps ownership and escalates to the site manager.

glossary.more: Width, slope, surface, level changes and protruding objects are set by the accessibility rules that apply to the site.

glossary.plain: A harm caused by the change itself, such as a new trip edge or harder cart pushing.
glossary.more: Pilots must look for and report adverse effects as well as benefits.

glossary.plain: Counts and rates about groups, never about named people.
glossary.more: This workspace only holds aggregate, non-identifying planning information.

glossary.plain: The official body that decides which rules apply to a site and whether work is allowed.
glossary.more: Often a building, fire or health official; there can be several for one site.

glossary.plain: How things are before you change anything, so later changes can be compared.
glossary.more: Gate G1 records the baseline, its quality and its limits.

glossary.plain: The zone from the floor to 120 cm where the kit looks for edges and corners at young children's height.
glossary.more: Set from WHO growth standards [S37]: tall five-year-olds are about 118–119 cm (97th percentile). Raise it for older children.

glossary.plain: A short code that points to a record kept in a protected system, instead of copying the details here.
glossary.more: For example INC-REF-0042 rather than a child's name or injury.

glossary.plain: Similar sites or periods without the change, used to judge whether the change made a difference.
glossary.more: Without one, a drop in incidents may be chance or a trend.

glossary.plain: A rule built into the page that stops it loading or sending anything over a network.
glossary.more: It is how the workspace keeps its no-network promise; you can read it in the page source.

glossary.plain: A checkpoint where named people decide, with evidence, whether work may continue.
glossary.more: Seven gates, G0 to G6, run in order. A gate reopens if its evidence changes.

glossary.plain: How much bigger a study must be because sites, not single visits, are compared.
glossary.more: A design effect of 2 doubles the number of events needed.

glossary.plain: Dynamic coefficient of friction: a measure of how slippery a hard floor is while something slides on it.
glossary.more: Results depend on the method, the device and the conditions; a number alone is not a safety verdict.

glossary.plain: One year of healthy life lost to illness, disability or early death.
glossary.more: WHO's falls fact sheet uses it to describe the burden of falls [S45].

glossary.plain: A trick where text in a spreadsheet cell runs as a formula when the file is opened.
glossary.more: The workspace adds an apostrophe to risky cells on export and removes it on import.

glossary.plain: Something that could hurt someone, such as a wet patch, a loose mat or a sharp shelf corner.
glossary.more: The hazard register records the hazard, who it affects and what was done.

glossary.plain: A database built into your browser, where this workspace keeps your planning work on your own device.
glossary.more: If the browser does not allow it, the workspace falls back to simpler browser storage, then to memory only.

glossary.plain: The place whose laws apply: a country, state, province or city.
glossary.more: Most rules in this kit are U.S. or Canadian worked examples; other places need their own review.

glossary.plain: Not favouring any product or material; the kit says what a solution must achieve, not what to buy.
glossary.more: Products are compared against written performance criteria (document 08).

glossary.plain: Future costs and savings added up in today's money.
glossary.more: A discount rate turns later amounts into present amounts; the calculator shows ranges, not a forecast.

glossary.plain: Describing what has to be achieved, and how it will be checked, instead of naming a product.
glossary.more: Acceptance criteria are written before buying anything (gate G3).

glossary.plain: A small, time-limited trial at a few sites, with a plan to stop or reverse it if needed.
glossary.more: A pilot tests whether a change can be run well; it usually cannot prove fewer injuries.

glossary.plain: Imagining that a plan has failed and listing the reasons, before you start.
glossary.more: Used in the adaptation kit to find harms early.

glossary.plain: Something sticking out into a walking route, such as a shelf edge or sign, that a person may not see.
glossary.more: Accessibility rules limit how far objects may protrude at certain heights.

glossary.plain: When saved work cannot be read, the workspace keeps an untouched copy and stops saving over it.
glossary.more: You can download the copy, then start fresh or import a backup.

glossary.plain: One rate divided by another; 0.8 means 20% lower.
glossary.more: Used in evaluation planning to describe the change you want to detect.

glossary.plain: Money set aside in advance to take a change out again if it causes problems.
glossary.more: Required before installation so that stopping is always affordable.

glossary.plain: A small browser helper that keeps a copy of the workspace files so a hosted copy opens without a connection.
glossary.more: It is used only when the workspace is served from a secure web address; it never stores your planning data.

glossary.plain: How well a floor stops feet from sliding.
glossary.more: It changes with water, cleaning products, wear and footwear, so it is checked in use, not only in a lab.

glossary.plain: The chance that a study detects a real effect of the size you care about.
glossary.more: Small pilots usually have low power for injuries, which is why the kit sets realistic aims.

glossary.plain: Systematic collection of injury counts, for example from hospital emergency departments.
glossary.more: It counts injuries; it does not watch people. Store CCTV is a separate, sensitive matter.

glossary.plain: A device that measures how slippery a floor is.
glossary.more: Different devices give different numbers; the method must be validated and agreed in advance.

glossary.plain: No injuries recorded during a period.
glossary.more: Zero events are not proof of safety: small pilots often see none either way.

discover.what: A short introduction to the program and the six stages of the journey.
discover.why: Most people decide in a minute whether something is worth their time.
discover.how: Read the summary, pick a stage, or answer three questions to find your starting point.
discover.life: Share it with a colleague or read the child-friendly version together with a child.
discover.outcome: You know what the kit is, what it is not, and where to go next.
discover.technical: The background image is generated in your browser and pauses when hidden, on low battery or with reduced motion.
discover.uncertain: The kit has not yet been evaluated for its effect on injuries.

start.what: Your starting point: a few questions, then the steps that fit your role and your goal, plus each role's first-day tasks.
start.why: The package is large; nobody needs all of it on day one.
start.how: Answer the questions. Each suggestion says why it was chosen. Then open your role for today's tasks and hand-offs.
start.life: Use it in a first meeting to agree who does what.
start.outcome: Two to five next steps, and a list of what you can safely skip for now.
start.technical: Suggestions come from fixed rules in source/content.json (startRules), so the same answers always give the same steps.
start.uncertain: The rules are a sensible default, not advice for your situation.

brief.what: A two-page brief for officials, with draft French and Spanish versions.
brief.why: Officials need the problem, the offer, the limits and the decisions that stay with them, quickly.
brief.how: Read it on screen, print it, or download a copy. Switch language at the top.
brief.life: Attach it to a briefing note, or use it to open a conversation with colleagues.
brief.outcome: A shareable summary that cites its sources.
brief.technical: The brief is documents 50 to 52; you can edit a local draft in the library.
brief.uncertain: The French and Spanish versions are draft translations that no native speaker has reviewed yet.

glossary.what: Plain-language definitions of the terms used in this kit.
glossary.why: Technical words should never stop someone from taking part.
glossary.how: Search or scroll. Each term links to where it matters.
glossary.life: Use it when preparing a meeting with people from other fields.
glossary.outcome: Shared words for businesses, officials, workers and researchers.
glossary.technical: The glossary is also document 55 in the handbook.
glossary.uncertain: Definitions are simplified; the cited documents carry the detail.

library.what: All documents and templates, with search and local drafts.
library.why: This is the full content of the program.
library.how: Filter by role or search. Open a document to read, print or edit a local draft.
library.life: Adapt a template, such as the pilot charter, for your site.
library.outcome: Documents you can print, edit and compare with the original.
library.technical: Documents are Markdown files; drafts are saved in this browser and flagged when the original changes.
library.uncertain: Many documents use U.S. and Canadian rules as worked examples.

doc.why: Each document does one job, such as a checklist, a form or a plan.
doc.how: Read it, print it, or edit a local draft and compare it with the original.
doc.life: Use your draft in meetings; export the working handbook to share it.
doc.outcome: A document you can use as it is or adapt.
doc.technical: Bracketed codes such as [S12] link to the source register.
doc.uncertain: Drafts are yours; they are not reviewed by anyone else.

evidence.what: Every claim the program makes, with its sources, limits and what it means for practice.
evidence.why: Honest limits protect children, businesses and officials from false confidence.
evidence.how: Filter by category. Read the limits column before quoting any claim.
evidence.life: Check a claim before putting it in a proposal or a press release.
evidence.outcome: Claims you can repeat with their caveats.
evidence.technical: Categories: verified source fact, program recommendation, illustration and unresolved.
evidence.uncertain: Evidence for children in retail settings is thin; most studies come from other settings.

sources.what: The source register: every source with jurisdiction, edition, retrieval date, access level and limits.
sources.why: A citation is only useful if you know what it covers.
sources.how: Search or filter. Open the link to read the source yourself.
sources.life: Re-check a source before relying on it in a decision.
sources.outcome: A list you can verify, with notes on what was and was not read.
sources.technical: Sources older than a year since retrieval are marked for re-checking.
sources.uncertain: Paid standards were read only at their public scope pages.

workflows.what: Step-by-step cards for each piece of work, with owner, authority, inputs, steps and escalation.
workflows.why: Clear ownership prevents both inaction and unauthorised action.
workflows.how: Open a card. Follow the steps and record the output in the named register.
workflows.life: Use a card to brief a new team member.
workflows.technical: Cards are generated into document 49 for print.
workflows.uncertain: Timings marked as program defaults need local confirmation.

pathway.what: How the program can grow from one site to many places, and how different organizations can help.
pathway.why: Spreading too fast, or without evidence, can cause harm and waste.
pathway.how: Find your organization in the table of ways to help. Check the evidence needed before each step.
pathway.life: Use it to plan a partnership or a funding proposal.
pathway.outcome: A responsible route to wider use, and concrete actions for helpers.
pathway.uncertain: No partner, funder or endorsement exists yet; the pathway is a proposal.

plan.what: The implementation plan: 35 tasks across seven gates, with owners, due dates and evidence.
plan.why: Tasks turn intentions into accountable work.
plan.how: Filter by gate or kind of work. Record status and an evidence reference for each task.
plan.life: Review the plan at each team meeting.
plan.outcome: A live task list that shows what blocks each gate.
plan.technical: Only status or evidence changes reopen a completed gate.
plan.uncertain: Task wording is general; adapt it to your site.

gates.what: The seven decision gates and what each needs before it can be recorded as complete.
gates.why: Gates stop work from running ahead of approvals and evidence.
gates.how: Complete the tasks, then record the gate with a decision reference. Amend if something changes.
gates.outcome: A clear record of what was decided, when and on what evidence.
gates.technical: Recording a gate here is not a signature; signatures live in your controlled systems.
gates.uncertain: Whether a gate is truly met is a human judgement.

registers.what: Planning registers: hazards, actions, decisions and 21 more, with fictional examples.
registers.why: Registers keep facts in one place so people can check them.
registers.how: Pick a register, add rows, or import a CSV file. Export to share.
registers.life: Run the hazard walk with the hazard register open on a tablet.
registers.outcome: Structured, non-sensitive records you can export.
registers.technical: Exports neutralise spreadsheet formulas; imports are previewed and can be undone.
registers.uncertain: The personal-data check finds common patterns, not every name.

calculator.what: Cost scenarios: net present value with ranges and best and worst combinations.
calculator.why: Decisions need costs and uncertainty, not a single hopeful number.
calculator.how: Enter your own assumptions and a basis for any savings. Read the ranges, not just the middle.
calculator.life: Bring the cash-flow table to a budget meeting.
calculator.technical: Discounting, escalation, replacement, salvage, withdrawal and removal costs are included.
calculator.uncertain: Results are only as good as the assumptions; they are not forecasts.

evaluation.what: Evaluation planning: how many events and visits a study would need, and what zero events can and cannot show.
evaluation.why: Most pilots are too small to prove an injury reduction; it is better to know that early.
evaluation.how: Enter the baseline rate and the change you want to detect.
evaluation.life: Use it before promising results to a funder or a council.
evaluation.outcome: A realistic aim for your pilot.
evaluation.technical: Uses the normal approximation for rate ratios and an exact Poisson upper bound for zero events.
evaluation.uncertain: Assumes stable rates and independent events; real data are messier.

adapt.what: A kit for adapting the program to another country, region or organization.
adapt.why: Laws, standards, languages and institutions differ; copying U.S. or Canadian rules would be wrong.
adapt.how: Work through the eight steps. Record what you find in the jurisdiction, standards, consultation and decisions registers.
adapt.life: Use it to start a national or municipal working group.
adapt.outcome: A local version you can defend, with its rules, consultations and translations recorded.
adapt.technical: This is document 53. International references are in the source register (S45 to S56).
adapt.uncertain: This kit cannot tell you which laws apply in your country.

data.what: Everything this workspace keeps in your browser, and controls to export, import, check and erase it.
data.why: Your planning data belong to you and should never leave your device by surprise.
data.how: Check where data are stored, export a backup, or erase selected parts.
data.life: Export a backup before changing computer or browser.
data.outcome: Control over your data, with nothing hidden.
data.technical: Planning data live in the browser database (IndexedDB); settings live in local storage; nothing is sent anywhere.
data.uncertain: Browsers can clear stored data; keep backups in an approved place.

about.what: Credits, licences, privacy and how the workspace is built.
about.why: You should know who made this, what it relies on and what it does not do.
about.how: Read the credits and the Zero Harm & Anti-Coercion commitments.
about.life: Check licences before copying or republishing.
about.technical: No third-party code runs in the workspace. Test tools are listed but not shipped.
about.uncertain: The package licence has not yet been chosen by the owner.

notfound.what: A page that does not exist in this workspace.
notfound.why: Links can break when documents are renamed or copied.
notfound.how: Use search or go back to Discover.
notfound.life: If a colleague sent the link, ask which version of the workspace they use.

discover.headline: Look again, from a child's height.
discover.lede: Child-Safer Spaces is a free planning kit for shops and public buildings. It helps the people who run them find and fix what makes children slip, trip, fall or hit their heads, without making the space harder for anyone else to use.
discover.band: Survey band 0–120 cm. Tall two-year-olds are about 92–93 cm and tall five-year-olds about 118–119 cm (WHO growth standards, 97th percentile) [S37].
kitIs: A planning kit: checklists, templates, workflows and decision gates.
Performance-based and material-neutral: it says what a fix must achieve, not what to buy.
Offline and private: no accounts, no network, no tracking. Your work stays on your device.
Free to read and try; a licence for reuse is still to be chosen by the owner.
kitIsNot: Not a standard, a certification, legal advice or an approval.
Not proven to reduce injuries: no outcome evaluation has been completed.
Not a reason to collect data about children, carers or workers.
Not a product endorsement: soft flooring, foam and playground tests do not establish safety in shops.
readaloud: Shops can be busy places, with carts, shelves and shiny floors.
Sometimes a floor gets wet, or a corner sticks out where small people walk.
The grown-ups who look after shops can crouch down and look from your height to find those spots.
Then they fix them, so everyone can walk around safely, including people who use wheelchairs.
If you see a spill or something sticking out, tell the grown-up you're with, or someone who works there.
claims: A narrow statement supported by a cited source, such as [S45].
A number calculated from your own assumptions, such as a cost scenario. Not a forecast.
What this program recommends. You may disagree and adapt it.
Invented examples (site EX-001) or imagery, such as the light on this page. Not data.
